pages.text: At a durbar, a drummer strikes the two great atumpan drums. Far across the park, people feel each beat in their chests before they have thought about hearing it. Rest a fingertip lightly on a drum skin as it is played and you will feel it trembling. Every sound begins this way. Something vibrates: a drum skin, a guitar string, the air inside a flute, or the vocal cords in your throat. A vibration is a quick, repeated movement to and fro. Stop the vibration by pressing your palm on the drum, and the sound stops at once.

pages.text: A vibrating drum skin pushes on the air particles next to it. They push on their neighbours, which push on theirs, and so a sound wave travels outwards. The particles themselves only shake to and fro. Sound therefore needs a material to carry it. That material is called a medium, and it may be a gas, a liquid, or a solid. Sound travels at about 340 metres per second in air, about 1,500 in water, and about 5,000 in steel. Where there are no particles, as in the vacuum of space, sound cannot travel at all. Space is completely silent.

pages.text: Two measurements describe a sound. Frequency is the number of vibrations each second, measured in hertz (Hz). It sets the pitch. A short, tight string vibrates quickly and gives a high note. A long, slack one gives a low note. Young people can hear from about 20 Hz to about 20,000 Hz. Amplitude is the size of the vibration, and it sets the loudness. Hit a drum harder and the skin moves further, so the sound is louder. The atumpan is a pair, one low-pitched and one high-pitched. By mixing them, a skilled drummer copies the rise and fall of spoken Twi and sends messages.

pages.text: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). A whisper is about 30 dB, ordinary talk about 60 dB, and heavy traffic about 85 dB. Speakers at a street party can pass 100 dB. Sound that is unwanted or harmful is called noise. Ghana has rules about it. In areas where people live, the limit is 55 dB in the daytime and 48 dB at night, from ten o’clock in the evening to six in the morning. Churches, mosques, and places of entertainment are allowed 65 dB by day and 60 dB at night. Many loudspeakers break these limits every week.

pages.text: Why do the limits matter? Deep inside each ear is a coiled tube lined with thousands of tiny hair cells. They turn vibrations into signals for the brain. Very loud sound, or loud sound that goes on for hours, flattens and kills these cells, and they never grow back. The hearing loss is permanent. Too much noise also steals sleep, raises stress, and makes it hard to learn. Protect your ears. Keep earphones at a moderate volume, stand well away from big speakers, and give your ears quiet time. Workers at mills and in mechanics’ yards should wear ear protection.

pages.text: Is silence the absence of all sound? Not quite. People who are deaf do not live outside the world of vibration. Many enjoy music by feeling its beat through the floor, a balloon held in the hands, or the body of a drum. Deaf dancers follow rhythms in this way. Deaf people in Ghana also share a full language of their own, Ghanaian Sign Language, which uses the hands, face, and body in place of the voice. Sound is one way of sensing vibration, and there are others. So look after your hearing, and learn a few signs. Communication is far bigger than sound.
